analogy.p: Imagine a line of buckets passing water down a row of people. The first person (the producer) fills a bucket, but only a tiny amount is collected. At each hand-over most of the water spills, soaks into clothes or evaporates, and only about a tenth reaches the next person's bucket. By the fourth person there is hardly a cupful left, so a fifth person would have nothing. This maps onto the biomass pyramid: each bucket is a trophic level, spilled water is biomass lost as waste, uneaten parts and respiration. The analogy breaks down because spilled water is simply wasted, whereas in an ecosystem the lost biomass is not wasted: faeces and dead material feed decomposers and the carbon is cycled back to producers.

bullets: Biomass is measured in units such as **kg, g or tonnes**, often per unit area (for example kg per m2) so that different areas can be compared fairly.
**Dry mass** is a more reliable measure than fresh (wet) mass because the water content of an organism changes with the weather and how recently it drank.
Measuring dry mass means killing the sample, so ecologists use small representative samples and scale up.
Biomass is the material that builds new tissue: growth of a consumer is the stored biomass that is left after all the losses in this topic.
Biomass is made by producers from carbon dioxide and water during **photosynthesis**, which is why all biomass in a food chain starts with plants and algae.
Energy is stored in this biomass in chemical bonds; when biomass is lost, the energy it contains is lost from the food chain too.
In AQA questions, 'biomass' and 'mass of living material' are interchangeable phrases, so use either.
core.h: What biomass is and how it is measured
core.p: **Biomass** is the mass of living material (organic matter) in organisms, or in a trophic level, in an area. Because living things contain very variable amounts of water, ecologists usually compare **dry mass**: the organism is dried in an oven until its mass stops falling, so only the organic material and not the water is measured. Biomass is the 'currency' that is passed along a food chain when one organism eats another, so tracking it tells us how much living material is available at each stage.

bullets: Producers are the source of all biomass entering a food chain.
Primary consumers eat producers; secondary consumers eat primary consumers; tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.
Arrows in a food chain point in the direction of **transfer of biomass (and energy)**, from the organism being eaten to the one that eats it.
An organism can sit in more than one trophic level in a food web, for example an omnivore eating both plants and animals.
Food chains seldom have more than four or five trophic levels, and this topic explains why.
Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) release nutrients back into the soil and are part of the cycling of materials.
core.p: Each feeding stage in a food chain is a **trophic level**. Level 1 is always the **producers**, usually green plants or algae, which make their own food by photosynthesis. Level 2 contains the **primary consumers** (herbivores), level 3 the **secondary consumers** (carnivores that eat herbivores) and level 4 the **tertiary consumers**. The final consumer in a chain is the **apex predator**, which has no predators of its own. **Decomposers** break down dead material from every level and are not normally drawn as a level in a pyramid.

bullets: Bars are stacked **centred on a vertical line**, producers at the base, so the diagram forms a pyramid shape.
The bar for each level is drawn to a suitable scale, for example 1 cm = 1000 kg, and each bar is labelled with the organism and the trophic level.
Only the **relative** sizes matter: the pyramid shows how biomass falls at each step up the chain.
To construct one you need biomass data (dry mass) for each trophic level, found by sampling and scaling up to the area studied.
Pyramids of biomass are almost always pyramid-shaped, because biomass is lost at every transfer (explained in the next sections).
A pyramid of biomass can be used to compare communities, for example before and after farming or pollution.
Check the units and the scale on exam diagrams before reading values; a bar that looks bigger may represent a different scale.
core.h: Pyramids of biomass: what they show
core.p: A **pyramid of biomass** is a diagram showing the relative amount of biomass at each trophic level in a food chain. Each trophic level is drawn as a horizontal bar, with producers at the bottom and the top consumer at the top. The width (length) of each bar is drawn **to scale** and is proportional to the total dry mass of all the organisms at that level. Unlike a pyramid of numbers, it accounts for the size of organisms, so it gives a true picture of how much living material is available to the next level.

bullets: Not all the organism is **eaten**: some parts such as roots, bones, shells, hair or fur are not eaten or not digestible.
Not all that is eaten is **absorbed**: some passes out as **faeces** (egestion), which still contains biomass that goes to decomposers.
Some absorbed material is lost as **urine** (urea and water) in excretion.
Much of the absorbed glucose is used in **respiration**, which releases carbon dioxide and water to the environment and provides energy.
Energy from respiration is used for movement, for keeping warm (mammals and birds) and for other life processes, and ends up as **heat** lost to the surroundings.
Only the biomass left over after all of these losses can be used to **grow** new tissue and so be available to the next consumer.
So at each step up, the amount of biomass transferred is roughly one tenth of what was available at the level below.
core.h: Why biomass falls at each trophic level
core.p: Only a small fraction, **approximately 10%**, of the biomass at one trophic level is transferred to become biomass in the next level. The rest is lost to the environment or never taken in at all. This is why each bar in a pyramid of biomass is much smaller than the one beneath it. The key idea for exam answers is that **not all the biomass eaten becomes new biomass in the consumer**, and **not all of an organism is eaten**.

bullets: **Parts not eaten**: bones, teeth, hair, fur, shells, feathers, and for plants roots and woody stems. This biomass stays in the lower trophic level (and later goes to decomposers).
**Waste materials**: faeces (undigested food) and urine. Faeces contains biomass that was eaten but not absorbed.

**Respiration**: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water (+ energy). The carbon dioxide and water leave the organism by breathing out, sweating and in urine, so their mass is lost from the food chain.
**Movement and keeping warm** use energy from respiration, so more active animals and those that maintain a constant body temperature lose more.
Large losses mean a large amount of food must be eaten for a small amount of growth.
The lost energy is not recycled in the food chain: it is transferred to the surroundings as heat, which is why we say energy flows through ecosystems while materials (carbon, water) are cycled.
Higher-level exam link: losses explain why food chains are short and why top predators are rare.
core.h: The losses in detail: respiration, waste and uneaten parts
core.p: Examiners reward answers that name the specific losses and link them to the lost mass. There are three main routes by which biomass fails to reach the next trophic level. First, part of the organism is never eaten. Second, part of what is eaten is lost as waste material. Third, much of what is absorbed is broken down in respiration to provide energy, and the mass leaves as carbon dioxide and water.

bullets: **Efficiency (%) = (biomass transferred to the next level / biomass available at the previous level) x 100**.
The same formula is used for energy: efficiency = energy transferred / energy available x 100.
Rearranged to find the biomass transferred: **biomass transferred = efficiency/100 x biomass available**.
Rearranged to find the biomass available: **biomass available = biomass transferred / efficiency x 100**.
The answer is a percentage and is normally less than 100%; if you get more than 100 you have inverted the fraction.
Give the answer to the number of significant figures asked, or 2 significant figures if unsure, and always include the % sign.
You may be asked for efficiency as a fraction: for example 80 kg out of 800 kg is 80/800 = 1/10.
Worked check: 450 kg to 36 kg is 36/450 x 100 = 8%.
core.h: Calculating the efficiency of biomass transfer
core.p: The efficiency of transfer between two trophic levels is the percentage of the biomass available at one level that ends up as biomass in the next. Use the formula below, making sure both values use the **same units** and that the top of the fraction is the **higher** trophic level (the smaller number in a pyramid), and the bottom is the lower level that provides the food.

bullets: Reasons light energy is not used: **reflected** by the leaf surface, **transmitted** through leaves, absorbed by non-photosynthetic parts, or the wrong wavelength.
Other limits on photosynthesis include low carbon dioxide, lack of water, low temperature and shortage of minerals (see the photosynthesis topic).
Producers lose some of the glucose they make in their own respiration, so not all photosynthesis product becomes new plant biomass.
The remaining biomass is the amount available to primary consumers.
Because the producers' biomass is so important, anything that damages producers (disease, drought, pollution) affects every other trophic level.
The 1% figure is a general estimate of the transfer from light to biomass; the 10% figure is the typical transfer between consumers.
core.p: The bottom of every pyramid is limited by how efficiently producers capture sunlight. Producers transfer only about **1% of the incident energy from light for photosynthesis**. Much of the light is reflected, passes through leaves or is the wrong wavelength, and is not absorbed by chlorophyll; some warms the leaf or evaporates water. So the amount of biomass at the base of the pyramid is already small compared with the Sun's output, and further losses at each step leave very little at the top.

bullets: Biomass left at a level is roughly one tenth of the level below, so each level supports fewer, or smaller, organisms than the one below.
A tertiary consumer such as a hawk needs many hundreds of times its own biomass in plants to exist: for 1 kg of hawk biomass you need approximately 1000 kg of producer biomass (10 x 10 x 10).
Top predators have large territories because the food supply per unit area is so small.
If the number of producers falls, all consumers' populations are likely to fall because less biomass is passed on.
Removal of a top predator can cause a rise in the numbers of its prey, which can then reduce producers: this links to interdependence and stable communities.
Because so little biomass reaches the top, bioaccumulating toxins such as pesticides can be concentrated in top predators (link to pollution).
core.h: Consequences: short food chains and fewer top predators
core.p: Because roughly 90% of the biomass is lost at each step, the total biomass available falls very quickly along the chain. After four or five steps there is too little biomass left to support another trophic level. This explains why most food chains have **only four or five trophic levels** and why **top predators are few in number** and need a very large feeding area. It also explains why a change at the bottom of a food web spreads upwards.

bullets: Pyramids of numbers ignore the **size** of the organisms.
One producer (an oak tree) can support many consumers, so the number pyramid can be inverted or diamond-shaped.
Pyramids of biomass show the **mass** of living material, so they nearly always narrow at each level.
Pyramids of biomass are harder to construct because organisms must be dried and weighed (and this kills them).
Biomass pyramids compare communities more fairly because every level is measured in the same unit, kg.
In an exam, if asked why a pyramid of numbers is not a pyramid, say 'one producer is very large and supports many small consumers'.
core.h: Pyramids of biomass compared with pyramids of numbers
core.p: A **pyramid of numbers** counts the individual organisms at each level, regardless of size. It can produce odd shapes: for example, one large oak tree supports thousands of insects, giving a pyramid that is narrow at the base, wide in the middle. A **pyramid of biomass** takes the mass of the organisms into account, so the oak's large mass is shown correctly and the pyramid is the expected shape. This is why biomass pyramids are considered more accurate.

bullets: A crop eaten directly by humans makes humans a **primary consumer**, with only one transfer (about 10% of the crop biomass).
If the crop is fed to cattle and humans eat the cattle, humans are a **secondary consumer**, with two transfers (about 1% of the crop biomass).
So eating plants gives roughly **ten times** more food biomass per unit area than eating animals fed on the same plants (on these simple estimates).
Intensive farming (for example battery chickens or indoor cattle) reduces movement and heat loss, which raises the efficiency of biomass transfer.
Ethical issues arise: animal welfare, restricted space and cost against the need for cheap food.
Growing crops for humans needs less land, so it can help food security and leave more land for wildlife.
Higher-tier link: farmers must balance higher yields against environmental and ethical costs (see food security).
core.p: Because of the large losses at each transfer, a given area of land produces far more food for humans if people eat **plants directly** than if the plants are fed to animals which are then eaten. This is why meat production is less efficient in terms of land and resources. Farmers can increase efficiency by cutting down the losses: keeping animals in warm, restricted conditions so that less energy goes on movement and keeping warm.

bullets: Read each axis and the **unit** carefully: some questions give kg per m2 per year or kJ.
If asked to **draw a pyramid of biomass**, choose a scale, calculate each bar length, centre each bar on a vertical line, and label the levels.
To compare efficiencies in a table, calculate each percentage and state which is larger, quoting numbers.
If asked why efficiency is not exactly 10%, say that 10% is only an **approximate** average and values vary with the organisms and environment.
Use 'about' or 'approximately' with the 10% figure, since the spec states 'approximately 10%'.
When asked to explain a loss, always link the cause to the mass lost, for example 'carbon dioxide leaves in respiration so mass is lost'.
Be careful with 'energy' and 'biomass': they are related but not the same thing; matching the word in the question is safest.
core.p: Exam questions give biomass data in tables, bar charts or pyramids and ask you to calculate efficiencies, identify missing values or evaluate a statement. A systematic approach avoids errors: identify which two trophic levels are involved, write the formula, substitute, calculate and give the answer with the correct unit or percentage. Check that the answer is sensible: transfer efficiencies between consumers are usually around 10%.

bullets: **Respiration (4.4)**: the same reaction that releases energy for movement is why carbon dioxide and water leave the organism.
**Photosynthesis (4.4)**: producers make the biomass that starts every food chain, and limiting factors reduce it.
**Carbon cycle (4.7)**: carbon moves along food chains as biomass and returns to the atmosphere through respiration and decay.
**Food security (4.7, triple)**: shorter food chains and less wasteful farming methods can increase the amount of food available.
**Interdependence and stable communities**: a change in biomass at one level affects the populations at others.
**Maths skills**: percentages, ratios, scales, rearranging equations and drawing to scale.
core.p: Biomass transfer links ecology to many other parts of the specification. It explains the carbon cycle (carbon moves between organisms as biomass and returns to the air as carbon dioxide in respiration), it relates to the energy changes in respiration, and it underpins discussions of food security, sustainable farming and the effect of humans on ecosystems.

exam: **State (1 mark)** the percentage of biomass transferred: 'approximately 10%'. Say 'about', not 'exactly'.
**Describe/define (1-2 marks)** a pyramid of biomass: 'shows the relative biomass (dry mass) of organisms at each trophic level'.

**Calculate (2 marks)**: 1 mark for the correct substitution into efficiency = transferred/available x 100, 1 mark for the answer. Show every step; you can earn the method mark even if the arithmetic is wrong.
**Explain (2-3 marks)** why biomass decreases: name two losses (respiration/carbon dioxide, waste/faeces and urine, parts not eaten) and say that only the remainder is available.
**Explain (4 marks)** why food chains are short: losses at each level, only about 10% transferred, so not enough biomass/energy left to support more levels.
**6-mark evaluate**: compare crop eating with meat eating, using numbers from the data (for example 10% vs 1%), then add ethical, welfare or cost factors and reach a conclusion.
Use the **command words**: 'state' = short fact, 'describe' = say what happens, 'explain' = give the reason, 'calculate' = work out with working shown, 'evaluate' = weigh up.
For graph and pyramid questions, quote **values from the diagram** with units to support your point.
Draw bars **to scale**, centred and labelled, when asked to construct a pyramid; mark schemes give a mark for scale and a mark for labelling.
Round sensibly and check the answer is under 100%; check the units are consistent before dividing.

mistakes.r: Energy is **transferred to the surroundings** (as heat) and in waste; it is not destroyed.
mistakes.w: Energy is 'used up' or 'destroyed' at each level.

mistakes.r: Only about 10% is **transferred to the next level**; about 90% is lost.
mistakes.w: Only 10% of energy is lost at each stage.

mistakes.r: Biomass is lost through **uneaten parts, waste (faeces and urine) and respiration**.
mistakes.w: Biomass is lost because animals are eaten by predators.

mistakes.r: Carbon dioxide and water leave the organism, so **mass (biomass) is lost**.
mistakes.w: Carbon dioxide from respiration is not a loss of mass.

mistakes.r: Efficiency = **biomass in next level / biomass in previous level** x 100, so it is under 100%.
mistakes.w: Calculating efficiency with the larger number on top.

mistakes.r: Always include units: **%** for efficiency; kg for biomass.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the % sign or giving a fraction when a percentage is asked.

mistakes.r: A pyramid of numbers counts organisms; a pyramid of **biomass** shows the mass at each level.
mistakes.w: Saying a pyramid of numbers shows biomass.

mistakes.r: Food chains are short because **too little biomass is left** after repeated losses to support another level.
mistakes.w: Saying 'food chains are short because animals die'.

mistakes.r: Biomass is normally **dry mass** because water content varies.
mistakes.w: Using the wet mass for biomass.

summary: AQA triple biology asks you to construct and interpret pyramids of biomass, explain why only approximately 10% of biomass is transferred to the next trophic level (losses in respiration, waste and uneaten parts), and calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer. It matters because it explains why food chains are short and why eating plants is more efficient than eating meat, and calculation and 4 to 6 mark explanation questions are common.

terms.d: The mass of living material (organic matter) in organisms or a trophic level, usually measured as dry mass.
A feeding stage in a food chain, starting with producers at level 1.
An organism, normally a green plant or alga, that makes its own food by photosynthesis and is the source of biomass in a food chain.
An organism that eats producers (a herbivore).
An organism that eats primary consumers (a carnivore or omnivore).
An organism that eats secondary consumers.
A diagram showing the relative amount of biomass at each trophic level, drawn to scale with producers at the base.
A diagram showing the number of organisms at each trophic level, which ignores their size.
The mass of an organism after all water has been removed, used as a measure of biomass.
The percentage of biomass at one trophic level that becomes biomass in the next level.
The chemical reaction in cells that transfers energy from glucose, releasing carbon dioxide and water.
Removal of undigested food (faeces) from the body.
Removal of waste products of metabolism, such as urea in urine.
A microorganism such as a bacterium or fungus that breaks down dead material and waste.
Having enough food available to feed a population.
The top consumer in a food chain, with no predators of its own.

worked.ans: 9% (so about 9% of the grass biomass becomes caterpillar biomass).
worked.q: A field of grass has a producer biomass of 6000 kg. The caterpillars that eat the grass have a biomass of 540 kg. Calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer from grass to caterpillars. (2 marks)
steps: Efficiency = biomass transferred / biomass available x 100

worked.q: In a food chain, producers have 25000 kg of biomass. Assuming 10% is transferred at each stage, calculate the biomass of the secondary consumers. (2 marks)
A secondary consumer population has a biomass of 36 kg. This is 12% of the biomass of the primary consumers. Calculate the biomass of the primary consumers. (2 marks)
steps: Biomass available = biomass transferred / efficiency x 100
